setup.topic: The C preprocessor and separate compilation

history.tutor:
Building a C program from `main.c` and `util.c` takes three stages. The preprocessor handles every line that starts with `#`: it pastes the text of each included header into the file and expands macros, which gives one translation unit per `.c` file. The compiler turns each translation unit into an object file, `main.o` and `util.o`, on its own; a call to a function defined in the other file is left as an unresolved symbol. The linker joins the object files, matches every unresolved symbol to its one definition, and writes the executable. `util.h` is never compiled by itself: it exists only as text pasted into both translation units.

<note>Preprocessor: one `.c` file plus the text of its headers becomes one translation unit. Compiler: each translation unit becomes one object file, separately. Linker: the object files are joined and each symbol is matched to its definition.</note>

A `std::unique_ptr<T>` is always in one of two states: it owns an object, or it is empty and holds `nullptr`. `std::make_unique<T>()` gives you one that owns a new object; a default-constructed one is empty. Moving from an owner with `std::move` transfers the object to the destination and leaves the source empty. `release()` also leaves it empty, handing you the raw pointer without deleting anything. `reset()` deletes the object and leaves it empty. When an owning `unique_ptr` is destroyed it deletes its object; when an empty one is destroyed nothing happens. No operation produces two `unique_ptr`s that own the same object, which is why it cannot be copied.

<note>`std::unique_ptr<T>` is either owning or empty. Moving from it, `release()` and `reset()` all leave it empty; only `reset()` and the destructor delete the object. It can be moved but not copied, so an object has at most one owner.</note>

reply:
It would waste less memory and cost far more time. Growing by a fixed 10 slots means a new buffer every 10 `push_back` calls, and each new buffer has every element stored so far moved into it. Over 1,000 calls that is 10 + 20 + ... + 990 = 49,500 element moves, and the total grows with the square of the number of elements. With doubling the moves are 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + 512 = 1,023, always fewer than twice the number of elements. That is what makes `push_back` amortised constant time, which the standard requires. <grade verdict="correct" score="1">"const int n = 7;" is right: a `const` integer initialised with a constant expression can itself be used in constant expressions, so `sq(n)` can be evaluated at compile time.</grade>

<summary>**Score:** 2 of 3.

**Strengths:** what `constexpr` means on a function: it may be evaluated at compile time, and it still works as an ordinary function at run time. You also picked the declaration that fixes line B.

**Misconception to fix:** that a variable initialised with a literal is known to the compiler. In Question 2 you expected `constexpr int k = sq(n);` to compile with `int n = 7;`. What matters is whether the variable is `const` (or `constexpr`), not what it was initialised with.

**Review:** which expressions count as constant expressions, and the difference between a `constexpr` function, which may run at compile time, and a `constexpr` variable, which must be initialised at compile time.</summary>
